title: Ramdhvaj and the Rise of Debera
body: Udayaditya's murderer took the throne as Suklampha, with the Hindu name Ramdhvaj. He made Debera, the ringleader of the conspiracy, his Bar Barua. The Deori Chutiyas were subdued and made to pay a yearly tribute of boats, and the Mishmis gave up the men behind a raid. When the king fell ill, Debera feared the succession and had Ramdhvaj poisoned in March 1675.
key_facts: Ramdhvaj's Ahom name was Suklampha
Debera, leader of the plot, became Bar Barua
Deori Chutiyas paid a yearly tribute of boats
Ramdhvaj was poisoned by Debera in March 1675
image_query: Scheming minister in a dim palace corridor
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 160

title: Puppet Kings: Suhung and Gobar
body: Debera killed his opponents and set up Suhung from Samaguri as king. When Suhung tried to get rid of him, Debera had him assassinated after a reign of only 21 days, and then made Gobar, grandson of the Deo Raja, king. The Bar Phukan, Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain swore an oath together and marched against Debera, whose troops deserted him. He was executed, and Gobar was killed after barely a month.
key_facts: Suhung reigned only 21 days before Debera had him killed
Gobar was king for barely a month
Debera was overthrown and executed by the great nobles
image_query: Nobles swearing a solemn oath together
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 161

title: Sujinpha and the Two-Fold Oath
body: The nobles chose Sujinpha of the Dihingia clan, and his accession was celebrated for seven days. To guard against plots, he ordered all officers to swear fealty, which angered them. The Burha Gohain led a night attack on the palace, but the king rushed out sword in hand and drove the attackers off. Captured conspirators swore a two-fold oath: before Brahmans with a Salgram, the Bhagavat and a tulsi plant, and by shedding blood before the great drum in the old Ahom way.
key_facts: Sujinpha belonged to the Dihingia clan
He fought off a night attack sword in hand
Conspirators took both a Hindu oath and an Ahom blood oath before the great drum
image_query: King defending his palace with a sword at night
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 162

title: The Fall of Sujinpha (1677)
body: The Burha Gohain escaped by boat to Lakhau, gathered malcontents, refused a promise of pardon and defeated the king's troops at Sinatali. Sujinpha fled to Garhgaon but was seized; his eyes were put out and he was afterwards stoned to death in July 1677. Of his four sons, the eldest, Dighala, escaped, the second was blinded, and the two youngest were killed.
key_facts: The Burha Gohain defeated the royal troops at Sinatali
Sujinpha was blinded and killed in July 1677
He was buried at Charaideo
image_query: Boat escaping downriver at night
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 163

title: Sudaipha and the Mistaken Murder
body: The nobles urged the Burha Gohain to become king, but he was not of royal blood and the Bailong pandits objected. So Khamcheo of the Parbatiya clan was installed as Sudaipha. He married the Burha Gohain's daughter and loaded him with honours. The disgraced Belmela Phukan crept into the palace at night to kill the king, but in the darkness killed the king's mother by mistake.
key_facts: The Burha Gohain could not be king as he was not of royal blood
Khamcheo of the Parbatiya clan became king Sudaipha (1677–1679)
The Belmela Phukan killed the king's mother by mistake

source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 163

title: Laluk Bar Phukan Surrenders Gauhati (1679)
body: Threatened by the all-powerful Burha Gohain, the Bar Phukan secretly arranged with the Nawab of Bengal for Prince Muhammad Azam to take Gauhati, which he surrendered early in March 1679. He then raised an army, marched on the capital and by November 1679 was master of the kingdom. He had Sudaipha put to death and raised a young prince, Sulikpha, to the throne.
key_facts: The Bar Phukan surrendered Gauhati to the Mughals in March 1679
Prince Muhammad Azam took possession of Gauhati
Sudaipha was killed and Sulikpha made king
image_query: Fort gates opened to an enemy army
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 164

title: Lara Raja, the Boy King (1679–1681)
body: Sulikpha was known as Lara Raja, the boy king, because of his young age. His first act, prompted by the Bar Phukan, was to execute the Burha Gohain. The Bar Phukan, now all-powerful, began wearing garments only the king could wear, until the other nobles had him assassinated. To remove all rivals, Lara Raja had several hundred princes of the royal family killed or mutilated.
key_facts: Sulikpha was called Lara Raja, the boy king
The ambitious Bar Phukan was assassinated by the nobles
Several hundred royal princes were killed or maimed

subject: Assam History

source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 164

title: Gadapani in Hiding
body: One rival escaped Lara Raja: Gadapani, son of Gobar. He lived in hiding near Rani in Kamrup, in the house of a Garo woman, dressed as a common peasant and working in the fields. In July 1681 the Bar Phukan took up his cause. As the rebels advanced, Lara Raja's army melted away; he was caught, banished to Namrup, and later put to death for plotting to regain the throne.
key_facts: Gadapani was the son of Gobar
He hid near Rani in Kamrup in a Garo woman's house
Lara Raja was deposed in 1681

topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 165

title: Seven Kings in Eleven Years
body: In the eleven years after Chakradhvaj Singh's death, there were no fewer than seven kings, and not one died a natural death. Ministers like Debera, the Burha Gohain and Laluk Bar Phukan made and unmade kings. With the accession of Gadapani, this era of weak princes and ambitious ministers ended, and the Ahoms again presented a united front to their enemies.
key_facts: Seven kings in eleven years after Chakradhvaj Singh
None of them died a natural death
Gadapani's accession ended the era of intrigue
image_query: Seven crowns on a dark wooden table
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 166

title: Gadadhar Singh Takes the Throne (1681)
body: Gadapani took the Ahom name Supatpha and the Hindu name Gadadhar Singh, and made Barkola his capital. His first act was to equip an army to drive the Muhammadans out of Gauhati. He also dealt firmly with conspiracies early in his reign: accused nobles were tried by the three Gohains, and many plotters were executed or banished to Namrup.
key_facts: Ahom name Supatpha; Hindu name Gadadhar Singh
He reigned from 1681 to 1696
His capital was at Barkola
image_query: Strong king crowned in a hall
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 166

title: The Final Recovery of Gauhati (1682)
body: Gadadhar Singh's army met little opposition. The forts at Bansbari and Kajali fell at the first assault, and a great naval victory near the mouth of the Bar Nadi delivered the whole enemy fleet to the Ahoms. The Faujdar of Gauhati fled and was pursued as far as the Manas. A vast booty of gold, silver, elephants, horses and cannon was taken at Gauhati.
key_facts: Forts at Bansbari and Kajali fell at the first assault
Great naval victory near the mouth of the Bar Nadi
The Mughals were pursued to the Manas river
image_query: Brahmaputra river Guwahati
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 166

title: The Last Muhammadan War
body: This was the last war with the Muhammadans. From then on, both sides accepted the Manas river as the boundary. The Buranjis name the defeated general Mansari Khan, possibly from the word Mansabdar, meaning commander. Three cannon survive bearing the inscription that King Gadadhar Singh, having vanquished the Musalmans at Gauhati, obtained this weapon in 1604 Saka (1682 A.D.).
key_facts: The last Ahom–Mughal war ended in 1682
The Manas river became the accepted boundary
Cannon inscriptions record Gadadhar Singh's victory in 1682

subject: Assam History

source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 167

title: Miri and Naga Expeditions of Gadadhar Singh
body: In 1685 the Miris raided at night and burned the house of the Sadiya Khowa Gohain. A punitive expedition defeated them, and embanked roads with fortified gateways were built from the Brahmaputra to two forts in the Miri country. The Nagas of the Doyang valley submitted after their houses were burned, and a raid by the Namsang Nagas led to the capture of many, including their chief.
key_facts: The Miris raided in 1685
Embanked roads with fortified gates were built into the Miri country
The Namsang Nagas' chief was captured

subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 168

title: Why Gadadhar Singh Turned on the Gosains
body: The neo-Vaishnava sects founded on Sankar Deb's teaching had grown enormously. Their preceptors and followers claimed exemption from military service and public works, and the Sakta Brahmans at court exaggerated the problem. The king also feared his people would grow weak if they gave up meat and strong drink, and he bore a personal grudge against Gosains who had refused to shelter him while he was in hiding.
key_facts: Vaishnava followers claimed exemption from service and public works
Sakta Brahmans at court encouraged the king
Some Gosains had refused to shelter him while he was in hiding
image_query: Vaishnava monastery prayer hall
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 168

title: Persecution of the Vaishnava Sects
body: Many Gosains were sent to Namrup and put to death. The Auniati Gosain, Keshab Deb, escaped by hiding in a Chutiya village, but Ram Bapu, the Dakhinpat Gosain, was blinded and his gold and silver idols melted down. Low-caste disciples were hunted, robbed and forced to eat forbidden meat. When the persecution spread so far that no one with property was safe, the king ordered it stopped and ordered restitution.
key_facts: The Auniati Gosain Keshab Deb escaped by hiding
The Dakhinpat Gosain Ram Bapu was blinded
The king finally stopped the persecution and ordered restitution
image_query: Monk hiding in a village house
subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 169

title: Legacy of Gadadhar Singh (1696)
body: Gadadhar Singh died in February 1696 after a reign of fourteen and a half years. He broke the power of the nobles, restored the king's authority, drove the Muhammadans beyond the Manas and stopped the hill raids. A patron of Sakta Hinduism, he built the Umananda temple on Peacock Island opposite Gauhati, and the earliest known Ahom copper-plate land grants date from his reign.
key_facts: Gadadhar Singh died in February 1696
He built the Umananda temple on Peacock Island
The earliest Ahom copper-plate land grants date from his reign

subject: Assam History
topic: Intrigues and Gadadhar Singh (1673–1696)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 169

title: Gadadhar Singh's Land Survey
body: While hiding in Lower Assam, Gadadhar Singh had learned the Muhammadan system of land measurement. After his wars, he ordered a detailed survey of the kingdom, bringing surveyors from Koch Bihar and Bengal; it began in Sibsagar and was finished after his death. Fields were probably measured with a nal, a 12-foot bamboo pole, and the unit of area was the pura, four bighas of 14,400 square feet.
key_facts: The survey was based on the Mughal system of land measurement
Surveyors came from Koch Bihar and Bengal
Fields were measured with a nal, a 12-foot bamboo pole
The unit of area was the pura, equal to four bighas

subject: Assam History

source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 170

title: Rudra Singh Comes to the Throne (1696)
body: Gadadhar Singh's elder son succeeded him at Garhgaon as Sukhrungpha, with the Hindu name Rudra Singh. His father was buried at Charaideo with great ceremony: an effigy was dressed in fine clothes and given daily offerings of pigs, fowls, fish and wine. Rudra Singh reversed his father's policy: Brahman Gosains could return, provided they made the Majuli their headquarters, and the Auniati Gosain became his spiritual preceptor.
key_facts: Ahom name Sukhrungpha; Hindu name Rudra Singh
He reigned from 1696 to 1714
Majuli became the chief seat of the Vaishnava Gosains
The Auniati Gosain became the king's preceptor
image_query: Majuli river island monastery
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 171

title: Ghansyam and the Brick City of Rangpur
body: Rudra Singh wanted a palace and city of brick, but no one in his kingdom knew how to build them. He brought in an artisan named Ghansyam from Koch Bihar, who built many brick buildings at Rangpur near Sibsagar and at Charaideo. As Ghansyam was leaving, richly rewarded, he was found carrying a full written account of the country. Suspected of spying for the Muhammadans, he was put to death.
key_facts: Rudra Singh built a brick city at Rangpur near Sibsagar
The builder Ghansyam was brought from Koch Bihar
Ghansyam was executed as a suspected spy
image_query: Ahom brick palace ruins Sivasagar
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 171

title: The Kachari War Begins (1706)
body: The Kachari king Tamradhvaj boldly declared his independence, so Rudra Singh sent two large armies against him. The Bar Barua, with over 37,000 men, marched up the Dhansiri valley from Sala in December 1706, building forts along the way to protect his supplies. The Pani Phukan, with 34,000 men, went by way of Raha and the Kopili valley.
key_facts: Kachari king Tamradhvaj asserted his independence
The Bar Barua led over 37,000 men up the Dhansiri valley
The Pani Phukan led 34,000 men via Raha and the Kopili
image_query: Two armies marching into forested hills
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 172

title: The Capture of Maibong
body: The Kacharis made a feeble stand below Namira and again at Lathia hill, but fled before the Ahom forces. The Bar Barua entered the Kachari capital at Maibong unopposed and took a cannon and 700 guns. Meanwhile the Pani Phukan's army had to cut its way through dense jungle, sometimes managing little more than a mile a day, before joining him at Maibong.
key_facts: The Ahoms entered the Kachari capital Maibong unopposed
A cannon and 700 guns were captured
The Pani Phukan's army cut through jungle at about a mile a day
image_query: Maibong Kachari ruins Dima Hasao
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 173

title: Sickness at Maibong and the Return
body: At Maibong the troops suffered badly from the unhealthy climate and many fell ill, including the Bar Barua, who died on the way back. At the end of March 1707 the king abandoned his plan to take Khaspur. The Pani Phukan demolished the brick fort at Maibong, burned the town and set up a pillar thirteen feet high to mark the victory. The garrison left at Demera was withdrawn in the rains.
key_facts: The Bar Barua died of illness during the campaign
The Maibong brick fort was demolished in 1707
A 13-foot victory pillar was erected at Maibong

subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 174

title: The Jaintia King's Treachery
body: The Kachari king Tamradhvaj fled to Bikrampur and asked Ram Singh, Raja of Jaintia, for help. When the Ahoms withdrew, Ram Singh saw a chance to seize the Kachari kingdom. Under pretext of a friendly meeting at Balesvar, he captured Tamradhvaj and carried him off to Jaintiapur. Tamradhvaj sent a letter by a bairagi begging Rudra Singh to rescue him and asking forgiveness for his past offences.
key_facts: Tamradhvaj asked the Jaintia Raja Ram Singh for help
Ram Singh seized him at a 'friendly' meeting at Balesvar
Tamradhvaj begged Rudra Singh for rescue
image_query: King captured at a false peace meeting
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 174

title: Rudra Singh Invades Jaintia (1707)
body: Ram Singh refused to release his captive, so Rudra Singh closed the market at Gobha, on which the hill Jaintias depended, and in December 1707 sent two armies. The Bar Barua marched with 43,000 men through the Kachari country, while the Bar Phukan took the direct route through the Jaintia Hills. Ram Singh gave up Tamradhvaj, and his own nobles forced him to submit to the Bar Barua.
key_facts: Rudra Singh closed the Gobha market to pressure the Jaintias
The invasion began in December 1707
The Bar Barua led 43,000 men
Ram Singh's nobles made him submit
image_query: King riding alone to an enemy camp
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 175

title: The Bar Phukan's Fighting March
body: The Bar Phukan's army met real resistance in the Jaintia Hills. The Jaintias attacked at Athitbhaga and made a stronger assault with elephants at Lachor hill, where the Ahoms wavered but rallied. After waiting for fresh ammunition, the Ahoms stormed the Jaintia stockades at Buritikar hill on a day chosen by the astrologers, and then took three more stockades on the Barpani river.
key_facts: The Jaintias attacked with elephants at Lachor hill
The Buritikar stockades were stormed on an auspicious day
Three stockades on the Barpani river were taken

subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 177

title: Kachari and Jaintia Kingdoms Annexed (1708)
body: Rudra Singh ordered both captive kings brought to him and the Jaintia king's treasure divided among his troops. Ahom subjects who had fled to Khaspur during Mir Jumla's invasion were brought back, and an army of occupation stayed at Jaintiapur. In February 1708 envoys told the Muhammadan Faujdar of Sylhet that the Kachari and Jaintia kingdoms had been annexed to the Ahom dominions.
key_facts: Both captive kings were sent to Rudra Singh
Annexation announced to the Faujdar of Sylhet in February 1708
Refugees from Mir Jumla's time were brought back from Khaspur
image_query: Royal envoys on horseback with a message
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 177

title: The Jaintia Rising
body: The Jaintia nobles would not accept the loss of their king and independence. With the Raja of Khairam and two hundred Khasi villages, they attacked the eight forts left by the Bar Phukan, capturing three and killing the defenders. They also rescued the copper image of the goddess Jaintesvari that was being sent to Rudra Singh. Panic-stricken Ahom troops retreating to Gobha were cut down.
key_facts: The Jaintias were joined by the Raja of Khairam and 200 Khasi villages
Three of eight Ahom hill forts were captured
The copper image of Jaintesvari was rescued
image_query: Warriors ambushing a column in the hills
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 178

title: The Cost of the Jaintia War
body: As the rains approached, the Ahom commanders withdrew to Gobha, destroying Jaintiapur and killing a thousand of its inhabitants. The Ahoms lost 2,366 men, including twelve high officers. The booty included three cannon, 2,273 guns, 109 elephants and 12,000 pieces of silver from the Muhammadan, Ahom, Koch and Jaintia mints. Rudra Singh pardoned his commanders at the nobles' request.
key_facts: The Ahoms lost 2,366 men, including 12 high officers
Booty included 2,273 guns and 109 elephants
12,000 silver coins from four different mints were taken
image_query: Pile of captured silver coins and weapons
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 179

title: The Grand Durbar at Bishnath (1708)
body: In mid-April 1708 Rudra Singh received Tamradhvaj at a grand durbar in a tent held up by posts of gold and silver. The Kachari king crossed the Brahmaputra in the royal barge, rode an elephant with a golden howdah, and then approached on foot and knelt before the king. After a submissive reply, he was sent home with many presents. The Jaintia Raja Ram Singh died of dysentery in captivity.
key_facts: The durbar tent had posts of gold and silver
Tamradhvaj knelt before Rudra Singh and was allowed home
Jaintia Raja Ram Singh died of dysentery in captivity

subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 180

title: The Planned Invasion of Bengal (1714)
body: A few years later Rudra Singh prepared a new war against the Muhammadans, either for glory or, some say, to bring part of the sacred Ganges into his kingdom. He gathered a great army, fleet and all his cannon at Gauhati. The Kachari and Jaintia Rajas joined with 14,000 and 10,000 followers, and 600 Daflas came from the hills. But he fell mortally ill and died in August 1714.
key_facts: Rudra Singh planned to invade Bengal
Kachari and Jaintia Rajas joined with 14,000 and 10,000 men
He died at Gauhati in August 1714
image_query: Great army and fleet assembling at a river town
subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 180

title: Rudra Singh: Builder King
body: Many regard Rudra Singh as the greatest of all the Ahom kings. Though illiterate, he had a remarkable memory, intelligence and initiative. Besides the brick city at Rangpur, he built masonry bridges over the Namdang and Dimau rivers, the great Jaisagar tank and temple, the tank and temple at Rangnath, and several roads. The survey of Sibsagar was completed and Nowgong was surveyed.
key_facts: Regarded by many as the greatest Ahom king
He built the Jaisagar tank and temple
Masonry bridges were built over the Namdang and Dimau rivers

subject: Assam History

source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 181

title: Rudra Singh Opens Assam to the World
body: Rudra Singh partly abandoned the isolation policy of earlier kings. He is said to have received the submission of all the hill tribes and to have built up a large trade with Tibet. He sent envoys to other Indian rulers, studied foreign customs and adopted those he thought good. He brought craftsmen from Bengal, founded schools for Brahmans, and sent Brahman boys to study at the great centres of learning in Bengal.
key_facts: He established an extensive trade with Tibet
He sent envoys to other Indian rulers
Brahman boys were sent to study in Bengal

source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 181

title: Rudra Singh and the Sakta Guru
body: Wanting to become an orthodox Hindu by taking the sharan, Rudra Singh would not bow before one of his own subjects. So he summoned Krishnaram Bhattacharjya, a famous Sakta Mahant from Malipota near Santipur in Nadia, promising him the Kamakhya temple. The king then changed his mind, but when an earthquake shattered several temples he recalled the Mahant and ordered his sons and Brahmans to accept him as Guru.
key_facts: Krishnaram Bhattacharjya came from Nadia in Bengal
He was promised charge of the Kamakhya temple
An earthquake made Rudra Singh recall him

subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 182

title: The Five Sons of Rudra Singh
body: Rudra Singh left five sons: Sib Singh and Pramata Singh by one queen, Barjana Gohain by another, Rajesvar Singh by a third, and Lakshmi Singh by a fourth. Lakshmi Singh, being very dark, was no favourite with his father. Four of these sons later reigned in turn. Some say Rudra Singh's body was cremated, but the Ahom Buranjis state he was buried like his forefathers.
key_facts: Rudra Singh had five sons
Sib Singh, Pramata Singh, Rajesvar Singh and Lakshmi Singh all became king
The Buranjis say he was buried, not cremated

subject: Assam History
topic: Rudra Singh, the Great Ahom King (1696–1714)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 182

title: Sib Singh and the Parbatiya Gosains
body: Rudra Singh's eldest son Sib Singh took the throne at Rangpur as Sutanpha. He gave up the invasion of Bengal but obeyed his father's wish to become a disciple of Krishnaram Bhattacharjya. He gave him the hill temple of Kamakhya with large land grants, so Krishnaram and his successors became known as the Parbatiya Gosains. The modern Saktas of Assam are disciples of these Gosains.
key_facts: Sib Singh reigned from 1714 to 1744
Ahom name Sutanpha
Krishnaram's line became the Parbatiya Gosains of Kamakhya

source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 183

title: Phulesvari, the Queen Who Ruled (1722)
body: In 1722 Brahman astrologers predicted that Sib Singh's rule would soon end. To cheat fate, he declared his chief queen Phulesvari, renamed Pramatesvari, to be the Bar Raja, or chief king. He handed her the royal umbrella, the Ahom emblem of sovereignty, and had coins struck in both their names. Surviving coins confirm this: those of 1724 to 1731 bear his name and Phulesvari's.
key_facts: Phulesvari was made Bar Raja (chief king) in 1722
She took the name Pramatesvari
She was given the royal umbrella, the emblem of sovereignty
Coins were struck jointly in her name and the king's
image_query: Queen holding a royal umbrella
subject: Assam History
topic: Sib Singh to the Moamaria Rising (1714–1780)
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 183

title: The Insult That Led to Rebellion
body: Phulesvari's power was real, and she was even more devoted to Sakta Hinduism than her husband. Hearing that the Sudra Mahants of the Vaishnava faith refused to worship Durga, she had the Moamaria and other Gosains brought to a Sakta shrine and had the Sakta marks smeared on their foreheads with the blood of sacrificed animals. The Moamarias never forgave this insult, and half a century later they rose in open rebellion.
key_facts: Phulesvari was a zealous follower of Sakta Hinduism
She forced Vaishnava Gosains to wear Sakta marks in sacrificial blood
This insult led to the Moamaria rebellion fifty years later

title: Three Queens as Bar Raja
body: Phulesvari died in 1731. Sib Singh then married her sister Deopadi and made her Bar Raja under the name Ambika. After Ambika died about 1738, another wife, Enadari, renamed Sarbesvari, became Bar Raja in turn. The coins of the reign follow these changes, bearing Sib Singh's name together with each queen's.
key_facts: Phulesvari died in 1731
Her sister Deopadi became Bar Raja as Ambika
Enadari became Bar Raja as Sarbesvari

title: Hinduism Becomes Dominant
body: Sib Singh died in 1744. He built many temples and gave land to Brahmans with the generosity of a new convert; nineteen of forty-eight known Ahom copper-plate grants are his. Under him Hinduism became the predominant religion, and Ahoms who kept their old beliefs came to be looked down on. The Deodhais and Bailongs resisted, but people gradually took Hindu priests and gave up the free use of meat and strong drink.
key_facts: Sib Singh died in 1744
19 of 48 known Ahom copper-plate grants are from his reign
Hinduism became the dominant religion of the Ahoms

title: Sibsagar, Spies and the Pera Kagaz
body: Sib Singh is said to have run such an elaborate spy system that he knew everything done, or even said, in his kingdom. His public works included the Dhai Ali and the tanks and temples at Gaurisagar, Sibsagar and Kalugaon. Kamrup was surveyed, and the resulting register, the Pera Kagaz, listing all occupied lands and rent-free estates, still existed when the British arrived.
key_facts: Sib Singh built the tanks and temples at Sibsagar and Gaurisagar
He ran an elaborate system of spies
The Kamrup land register was called the Pera Kagaz

title: Four Europeans Visit Rangpur (1739)
body: In 1739 four Europeans, whose names appear to have been Bill, Godwin, Lister and Mill, visited Sib Singh at Rangpur. The king met them at the main gate of the city, where they are said to have paid him homage by falling at his feet.
key_facts: Four Europeans visited Sib Singh in 1739
Their names appear to have been Bill, Godwin, Lister and Mill
The king met them at the main city gate of Rangpur

title: Pramata Singh and the Rang Ghar (1744–1751)
body: Passing over Sib Singh's sons, the nobles made Rudra Singh's second son, Pramata Singh, king under the Ahom name Sunenpha. In 1745 a new survey and census were carried out. He built new buildings and masonry gateways at Garhgaon, the Rangghar, an amphitheatre for animal fights, at Rangpur, and the Rudresvar and Sukresvar temples at Gauhati. He was a kind ruler and died in 1751.
key_facts: Pramata Singh reigned 1744 to 1751
He built the Rangghar amphitheatre at Rangpur
He built the Rudresvar and Sukresvar temples at Gauhati

title: Rajesvar Singh and the Gendhela Bar Barua
body: Rudra Singh's third son was passed over because he was pitted with smallpox, and the fourth, Rajesvar Singh, became king. He built brick palaces at both Rangpur and Taimung. An able but pleasure-loving man, he left the government to his Bar Barua, Kirti Chandra Gendhela, whose overbearing manner soon made the other nobles hate him.
key_facts: Rajesvar Singh reigned 1751 to 1769
He built brick palaces at Rangpur and Taimung
Government was left to Bar Barua Kirti Chandra Gendhela

title: The Burning of the Buranjis
body: The Numali Bar Gohain wrote a Buranji casting doubt on the purity of Kirti Chandra's descent. The Bar Barua disproved it and argued that such writings might one day question even the king's origin. With the king's approval, all existing Buranjis were examined, and those containing anything objectionable were burnt. This made him even more unpopular, and a plot to assassinate him failed.
key_facts: The Numali Bar Gohain questioned Kirti Chandra's descent in a Buranji
Objectionable Buranjis were examined and burnt

title: The Dafla Blockade and the Duars Levy (1758)
body: In 1758 the Daflas raided near Ghiladhari. Forts were built along the frontier and the Daflas were barred from the plains; the blockade worked and they returned their captives. After an exchange of prisoners, an agreement let the Daflas collect each year from every family in the Duars, the tract along the foot of the hills, a pitra of paddy and 320 cowries, provided they stopped all other raids.
key_facts: The Daflas raided near Ghiladhari in 1758
A frontier blockade forced them to return captives

title: The Mikirs and the Kachari King Submit (1765)
body: In July 1765 two forces entered the Mikir hills from front and rear, defeated the Mikirs and burned their houses, and the Mikirs brought tribute and begged forgiveness. That November the Kachari king Sandhikari refused to receive Ahom messengers, but submitted when the Bar Barua marched to Raha. With him came Raja Jai Singh of Manipur, who had fled to him after the Burmese invaded Manipur.
key_facts: Two Ahom forces defeated the Mikirs in 1765
Kachari king Sandhikari submitted
Jai Singh of Manipur had been driven out by the Burmese

title: Restoring the Raja of Manipur (1768)
body: Rajesvar Singh agreed to help Jai Singh. The first expedition, sent through the hills south of Charaideo, struggled through dense jungle and had to turn back after many men died. In November 1768 a second force went by way of Raha and the Kachari country, and ten thousand men escorted Jai Singh as far as the Mirap river. He drove out the usurper placed on the throne by the Burmese and gave the king a daughter in marriage.
key_facts: The first Manipur expedition failed in the jungle
A second force went via Raha in November 1768

Manipuris were settled at Magaluhat near the Desoi

title: Signs of Approaching Decay
body: Rajesvar Singh died in 1769 after a twenty-day illness. Though indolent, he was capable, and his people enjoyed order and prosperity. But decay was near: the old warlike spirit had almost vanished, and for the first time high officers refused to go on active service. The people were priest-ridden, sectarian quarrels were growing, and the Moamaria Gosain was secretly spreading disaffection among his disciples.

title: Lakshmi Singh Becomes King (1769)
body: Kirti Chandra Bar Barua supported Rudra Singh's youngest son, Lakshmi Singh, claiming Rudra Singh had wished all his sons to reign in turn. Others backed Rajesvar's son and revived doubts about Lakshmi Singh's legitimacy. Lakshmi Singh, already fifty-three, was chosen and took the Ahom name Sunyeopha. He left affairs to the Bar Barua, who grew more arrogant than ever.
key_facts: Lakshmi Singh reigned 1769 to 1780
Ahom name Sunyeopha

title: The Spark of the Moamaria Rebellion
body: The Bar Barua heaped insults on the Moamaria Gosain for failing to salute him from the riverbank. Soon after, he had Nahar, chief of the Moran tribe and a disciple of the Gosain, beaten and his ears cut off for going to the palace before paying his respects. The Gosain resolved on rebellion, and his son Bangan led the disciples into Namrup, where the Morans and Kacharis hailed him and Bangan took the title Raja of Namrup.
key_facts: The Bar Barua insulted the Moamaria Gosain
Moran chief Nahar had his ears cut off
The Gosain's son Bangan became 'Raja of Namrup'

title: Ragha Captures the King (1769)
body: In October 1769 a Moran named Ragha, calling himself Bar Barua, led the rebels down the north bank and defeated the royal troops. Advised by his nobles, Lakshmi Singh fled Rangpur, but he was caught at Sonarinagar, brought back, and confined in the temple at Jaysagar. The rebels killed Barjana Gohain and the hated Kirti Chandra, along with his sons.
key_facts: Ragha, a Moran, led the rebel army
Lakshmi Singh was captured at Sonarinagar
The king was confined in the Jaysagar temple
Kirti Chandra Bar Barua was killed

title: Ramakant, King of the Rebels
body: The Moamaria Gosain forbade his son Bangan to take the throne and had Ramakant, a son of the Moran chief Nahar, made king instead. Coins were minted in Ramakant's name dated 1691 Saka (1769 A.D.), but the real power lay with Ragha. All the Gosains of Upper Assam were forced to accept the spiritual supremacy of the Moamaria high priest.
key_facts: Ramakant, son of Moran chief Nahar, was made king by the rebels
Coins were struck in his name in 1769

title: The Royalist Counter-Revolution (1770)
body: Learning that the rebels planned to kill the old officers and the king, the royalist leaders struck first while most rebels had gone home. In April 1770, on the night before the Bihu festival, Ragha's house was surrounded and he was killed; some say the Manipuri princess struck the first blow. Lakshmi Singh was restored, and the Moamaria Gosain and Ramakant were tortured and impaled.
key_facts: The royalists struck in April 1770, the night before Bihu
Ragha was killed; the Manipuri princess is said to have struck first
Lakshmi Singh was restored to the throne

title: More Rebellions under Lakshmi Singh
body: The harsh reprisals led to a fresh rising led by the Chungis of Namrup, who were beaten by mounted Manipuri mercenaries but kept up resistance from a fort deep in the forest. In December 1774 the dismissed Kalita Phukan proclaimed himself king as Mirhang, but his men deserted him and he was executed. In 1779 a Nara of Khamjang raised Chutiyas and Mishmis and killed the Sadiya Khowa Gohain.

The Kalita Phukan proclaimed himself king as Mirhang in 1774
Rebels killed the Sadiya Khowa Gohain in 1779

title: Death of Lakshmi Singh (1780)
body: Lakshmi Singh, shattered by the rising, died in December 1780 in his sixty-seventh year. The Deodhais blamed the country's misfortunes on Hindu practices and the cremation of Rajesvar, so they buried a clay effigy of him with the Rikkhvan ceremony and Ahom rites. The king built several temples and the great Rudra Sagar tank, and demolished the Talatulgarh for a bridge over the Dikhu that was never built.
